topology.actIAlt: Act I topology: the web client talks over REST to an intermediate layer, which communicates with three services over an internal binary protocol, and those services reach the database and the cache.

database.title: Modeling and performance
database.lead: Two engines, two different problems: designing a model that can absorb changing rules, and diagnosing one that is already in production.

columns.title: PostgreSQL · modeling
items: Schema definition, constraints, and referential integrity across a 62-entity model with soft delete.
Partial unique indexes written by hand where the ORM cannot express them.
Multi-entity transactions with the client propagated explicitly through the ports, and timeouts calculated from the real number of round trips.

columns.title: SQL Server · diagnostics
items: Analysis of blocking chains in production and their root cause: transactions left open by idle sessions.
Predicates that force full table scans and widen the scope of locks.
Reverse engineering and entity modeling over a legacy system of more than 1,300 tables and 5,000 stored procedures.

stack.title: Stack
notes: Third-party ERP integration: automating communication between external portals and applications against Odoo, over XML-RPC.
These levels reflect actual use, not familiarity. What is in the third level I built and then stopped using because of an architectural decision, not for lack of command over it.

about.title: About
paragraphs: I work on the design and development of internal systems at Grupo ROISA, an organization operating at scale in Buenos Aires. My work runs from the backend down to the database: APIs in NestJS, bulk-load processes against SQL Server, integration services in Python, and the data modeling of the platform replacing the company's legacy system.

I am studying Computer Engineering at Universidad Nacional de La Matanza, third year. Before that I trained as an aircraft maintenance technician. It sounds unrelated, but aircraft maintenance taught me something I use every day: procedures exist because failure is expensive and cannot be undone. Working against a production database with no rollback resembles that more than you would expect.

What interests me about this craft is the part a demo never shows: why a transaction boundary sits where it sits, what happens when the target system offers no atomicity, and what you give up when you choose one architecture over another.
